questions.prompt: The agent's changelog lists two behaviour changes. `git diff` shows a third: a default threshold moved from 40.0 to 45.0. What do you do?
questions.explain: The diff is the ground truth. A change the changelog omits is exactly what the routine exists to find, so you ask about it and decide to keep or revert it.

options.text: Ask the agent about the threshold, then keep or revert that line on purpose
Trust the changelog, since the agent wrote both and it knows what it meant
options.misconception: The changelog is the agent's account of its change. When it disagrees with the diff, the diff wins.

options.text: Ignore it: a number changing by five is too small to matter
options.misconception: A default threshold decides which records pass a filter. A small number can change results a lot.

options.text: Revert the whole change, since one omission means everything else is wrong
options.misconception: One gap does not make the other changes wrong. Question the gap and judge each change by itself.

questions.prompt: A colleague's notes on reviewing an agent's change. Which line is faulty?
questions.explain: The changelog is the agent's description of its own work, so it cannot settle a disagreement. Only the diff shows what changed.

lines.text: Ask for a changelog before keeping the change.
lines.why: It gives you a map for reading the diff.

lines.text: Check whether the diff holds anything the changelog leaves out.
lines.why: Omissions are the first thing to look for.

lines.text: If the changelog and the diff disagree, go with the changelog, because it explains the intent.
Write one sentence per change in your own words.
lines.why: A change you cannot explain is a change to question.

questions.prompt: Put the four-step routine in order.
questions.explain: You need the changelog before you can compare it, you must understand the change before you explain it, and you decide last.
items: Ask the agent for a changelog
Read the diff against the changelog
Explain each change back in your own words
Keep, edit or revert the change

why.Ask the agent for a changelog: Without it you have no map to read the diff against.
why.Read the diff against the changelog: Reading the diff comes before explaining, because you explain what the diff really does.
why.Explain each change back in your own wor: Explain-back comes after you have read the diff, and before you decide.
why.Keep, edit or revert the change: You decide once you understand the change.

questions.prompt: Compare the worked example's changelog with its diff. Sort each item.
questions.explain: Each claim has to be found in the diff. A claim with nothing behind it is overstated, and a diff line with no claim is omitted.

items.text: Lowercase bases now count towards GC
items.misconception: The diff adds `.upper()` to the sequence, so this claim is backed.
The diff adds a `len(r[1]) > 0` check in keep(), so this claim is backed.
The diff touches one file and adds no test, so the claim has nothing behind it.
This line is in the diff and absent from the changelog, so it was left out.

questions.prompt: An agent finishes a 600-line change across twelve files in one go. How do you apply the habit?
questions.explain: A changelog is only a map. When the diff is far too big to read, the fix is smaller pieces, each with its own changelog.

options.text: Ask for the work as small commits, each with its own changelog you can check
Ask for one changelog for the whole change and read only that
options.misconception: Then you never read the diff, and the changelog can still miss or overstate a change.

options.text: Skip the habit: it only suits small diffs
options.misconception: Large diffs are where understanding slips most. Cut them into pieces the habit can handle.

options.text: Ask the agent to confirm that nothing is missing, then accept it
options.misconception: The agent confirming its own account is not a check against the diff.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it is.
questions.explain: Keep the roles apart: the diff is the ground truth, the changelog is the agent's map, the explain-back is yours, and it can live in the commit.

pairs.right: The lines the change actually added and removed
pairs.misconception: The diff is the real record of the change, not anyone's description of it.

pairs.right: The agent's short account of what it changed and why
pairs.misconception: A changelog is the agent's own description. It can miss or overstate a change.

pairs.right: One sentence per change, in your own words
pairs.misconception: Explain-back is yours. Pasting the agent's text back does not show you understood.

pairs.right: A good home for your explain-back once you keep the change
pairs.misconception: The commit message is where the reason for a change is saved with the code.
